match.reason: The bank point covers burden and standard of proof in criminal trials only, with no civil claim content, so it does not teach that the plaintiff bears the burden and must prove the claim on the balance of probabilities.

draft.title: Principles of civil justice
card: In a civil case, one person or organisation sues another to fix a wrong, usually by getting money or another remedy. The person who sues is the plaintiff. The person sued is the defendant.
The plaintiff bears the burden of proof. This means the plaintiff must prove the claim. The defendant does not have to prove that the claim is false.
The standard of proof is the balance of probabilities. The plaintiff must show that their version of events is more likely than not to be true.
This standard is lower than in a criminal case, where the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. A civil plaintiff does not need to remove all doubt.
draft.remember: The plaintiff must prove the claim, and more likely than not is enough.

a.q: What must a plaintiff do to succeed in a civil claim?
opts: Show their version is more likely than not true
Show the defendant is guilty beyond reasonable doubt
Show that the defendant cannot disprove the claim
Show that the defendant broke the law on purpose
a.why: The plaintiff carries the burden of proof and meets it by showing their claim is more likely than not true. Beyond reasonable doubt is the criminal standard, so it is the tempting wrong option here.
a.clue: Think about who must prove the claim, and how strongly.

b.q: Priya sues Tom, a builder, for faulty work on her deck. At trial, the evidence leaves it about 60% likely that the work was faulty. Tom has not proved the work was sound. What is the result?
opts: Priya meets the standard, because it is more likely than not
Priya fails, because some doubt remains about the work
Priya fails, because Tom did not have to prove anything
Tom must lose, because he did not prove the work was sound
b.why: Priya has the burden of proof, and a 60% likelihood is more likely than not, so she meets the balance of probabilities. The last option is wrong because the burden stays with Priya, and she wins by meeting her own standard, not because Tom failed to prove anything.
b.clue: Does Priya need to remove all doubt, or only tip the balance?

a.best: Show their version is more likely than not true

b.best: Priya meets the standard, because it is more likely than not

problems.detail: Why (b) refers to 'the last option', but options are shuffled. Its reasoning ('not because Tom failed to prove anything') actually rebuts the option 'Tom must lose, because he did not prove the work was sound', not the option currently listed last ('Priya fails, because some doubt remains'). The explanation should name the option it rebuts by its content, not its position.
